summary.text: A 30-year-old man with Graves' disease, treated with propylthiouracil and propranolol for about a year, was referred to nuclear medicine in February 2024 after developing acute psychotic symptoms over the preceding month. He was moderately cachectic with an enlarged neck, bilateral exophthalmos, sweating, fine tremors and a heart rate of 125 beats per minute, and had paranoid ideation, hallucinations and disorganized behavior. He reported smoking 12 to 14 cigarettes per day and denied other major illnesses or a family history of hyperthyroidism or psychiatric disorders.

Laboratory tests showed suppressed TSH (<0.003 µIU/mL) and elevated free T4 (>5 ng/dL), and technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy showed diffuse increased uptake consistent with toxic diffuse goiter. A diagnosis of Graves' disease-associated psychosis was established, and the authors state the psychotic symptoms were caused by hyperthyroidism.

Given the severity of thyrotoxicosis he was pretreated for 7 days with methimazole and propranolol, with haloperidol, trihexyphenidyl and chlorpromazine started concurrently. He missed the 1-week visit and returned at 4 weeks, when thyroid function tests were repeated and psychiatric follow-up arranged. After a 3-day antithyroid drug withdrawal he received RAI at 370 MBq (10 mCi) while continuing psychiatric medications.

One month after RAI his hyperthyroid symptoms markedly improved and the psychiatric manifestations resolved completely, allowing gradual discontinuation of antipsychotics and return to work. Table 1 shows fT4 1.1 ng/dL and TSH 3.9 µIU/mL at 1 month and fT4 0.5 ng/dL and TSH 10.0 µIU/mL at 3 months after RAI. At 3 months he became hypothyroid and started levothyroxine. Psychiatric follow-up continued for 6 months after RAI with no further psychiatric medication required.
